body.text: On balance, Beijing has little reason to celebrate the United States’ midterm election results. The Democratic takeover of Congress complicates China’s strategic calculations, threatens some of the advantages Beijing has gained from President Donald Trump’s increasingly transactional foreign policy, and, perhaps most importantly, demonstrates something the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) would rather the world forget: U.S. democracy retains the capacity to correct itself.
Before explaining why, two qualifications are essential.

The first is that Trump’s departure from the traditional U.S. foreign policy consensus – which has long emphasized alliances, democratic values, multilateral institutions, and the defense of a rules-based international order – cannot be explained by Trump’s personality alone. Three structural developments have made an adjustment in U.S. foreign policy unavoidable.

The post-Cold War liberal international order has become increasingly expensive for the United States to maintain. U.S. allies have often depended excessively on U.S. security guarantees, while Washington’s domestic economic and fiscal pressures have grown. Meanwhile, China’s extraordinary economic, industrial, and military rise has fundamentally altered the global balance of power, making the unipolar arrangements of the 1990s increasingly unsustainable. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has exacerbated both problems, imposing additional security burdens on Washington while exposing the difficulty of maintaining international rules against determined revisionist powers.

The United States must adjust. Without Trump, that adjustment might have occurred more gradually, ideally allowing new institutions and responsibilities to emerge as the old order evolved. Instead, we are experiencing a dangerous period of international disorder in which established rules are breaking down faster than replacements can be constructed. Even after Trump leaves office, U.S. foreign policy neither can nor should return entirely to its pre-Trump form.

The second qualification concerns presidential power. Trump remains president for another two years. U.S. presidents enjoy considerable authority over foreign affairs, generally facing fewer congressional constraints than in domestic policymaking. A Democratic Congress cannot simply reverse Trump’s diplomacy with China, although it can pass legislation and budgets, increase oversight, and change political incentives. Any change is therefore more likely to be consequential at the margins than an immediate strategic reversal.
Nevertheless, Beijing has good reasons to view the midterm results with concern.

China prefers a transactional U.S. president to one guided by enduring principles and institutional commitments. During his first term, Trump surprised Beijing by launching a trade war that challenged decades of U.S. economic engagement. Chinese leaders initially struggled to understand his methods. Over time, however, Trump’s transactionalism became more pronounced, and Beijing learned to negotiate with him.

Trump has embraced the G2 language, signaling recognition of China as the United States’ principal peer competitor. He has treated Taiwan increasingly as a bargaining instrument, including through delays in arms sales. And he has accepted the language of “constructive strategic stability” advanced by Xi Jinping, opening the possibility of an understanding that prioritizes bilateral accommodation over traditional U.S. commitments.

Beijing recognizes the advantages of this approach. On November 2, the day before the midterms, the South China Morning Post, owned by Chinese conglomerate Alibaba Group, published an article titled “Will ‘strategic stability’ with China go out the window if Trump loses the midterms?” It warned that a Republican loss of the House could test the emerging strategic-stability framework. Yet it also expressed confidence that Trump would continue trying to stabilize relations with Beijing. The concern is revealing. Beijing has learned to work with Trump’s approach and would prefer that it remain largely undisturbed.

Congressional pressure could let values retake a place in U.S. China policy. It could also make Taiwan’s security less vulnerable to presidential bargaining. U.S. policy would remain pragmatic, but democratic values would be harder to exclude from relations with China.

Congress could also encourage the repair of the United States’ relationships with allies in Europe, North America, and the Indo-Pacific. Stronger cooperation with Canada, European democracies, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and other partners would reinforce the democratic world’s collective economic, technological, and military strength. Beijing benefits when Washington quarrels with its allies; it faces greater constraints when they coordinate.

The Iran war presents another consideration. Stronger congressional oversight could increase pressure to end the conflict sooner. China has little reason to welcome an early U.S. disengagement from a war that consumes Washington’s military resources, financial capacity, diplomatic attention, and political energy. A prolonged conflict distracts Washington from the Indo-Pacific and its strategic competition with China.

Advanced semiconductor exports provide an especially revealing example of where Congress could make a difference. Despite substantial bipartisan support for restricting China’s access to sensitive U.S. technology, Trump permitted sales of certain advanced Nvidia chips, including the H200, while retaining restrictions on the most sophisticated products. His administration connected these transactions to financial returns for the United States.

Republican congressional majorities had largely avoided directly confronting Trump’s decisions, despite objections from some China hawks. A Democratic Congress could be considerably more assertive, using hearings, legislation, and budgetary authority to tighten export restrictions. Beijing would certainly prefer fewer such constraints.

Trump’s second administration has generated serious controversies over executive power, the Iran war, sweeping tariffs, allegations of corruption and conflicts of interest, the handling of Epstein-related records, and the politicization of law enforcement. Critics see these developments as threats to constitutional government, the separation of powers, and the rule of law. These concerns deserve scrutiny through democratic institutions, with allegations distinguished from established wrongdoing.

As someone who has devoted much of his life to advancing democracy and human rights, I am particularly sensitive to democratic deterioration. I have heard from compatriots inside China that U.S. democracy has lost considerable appeal. Some friends have even joked that China’s official Xinhua News Agency no longer needs to fabricate negative stories about Washington. Its propagandists need only translate U.S. news reports. That observation contains a painful truth. The United Sates’ democratic weaknesses have provided authoritarian propaganda with powerful material.

Yet the midterm elections demonstrate something Beijing’s propagandists cannot easily explain away. Americans dissatisfied with their government’s direction have used the ballot box to change the balance of political power. The midterm elections created new opportunities for oversight and constitutional checks on the presidency.

On specific policy issues, one may agree or disagree with the voters who produced this outcome. That is not the essential point. The essential point is that U.S. democracy works. It retains the capacity to recognize mistakes, restrain power, and correct its course peacefully.

For Beijing, this is not a welcome result at all. A divided U.S. government can complicate Trump’s transactional diplomacy. A united democratic alliance can constrain China’s geopolitical ambitions. But a self-correcting U.S. democracy challenges something more fundamental: the CCP’s claim that authoritarian governance offers a superior political model.
